newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Roche sales show profits on target.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Roche sales show profits on target.

text.p: Roche Holding AG said on Thursday that 1996 sales rose 11 percent to 15.96 billion Swiss francs ($11.58 billion), confirming analysts' expectations that the Swiss pharmaceuticals group was on target to show a good rise in profits.
Roche's 1996 sales figures were in line with analysts' forecasts and confirmed that its pharmaceuticals division was still outperforming the rest of the market.
Most analysts left earnings forecasts unchanged after the sales figures, but a few adjusted numbers slightly upward.
"This is completely in line with expectations," said Mark Becker of J.P. Morgan.
After initial profit-taking, Roche's non-voting equity securities rebounded on the Swiss Exchange and closed 135 francs higher at 10,985 francs, a gain of 1.2 percent.

Sales from the pharmaceuticals division, critical for Roche's profitability, rose 10 percent in local currencies to 10.46 billion francs, comfortably above the market's average growth of around six percent.

Sales of Roche's leading products, such as Rocephin -- the world's top-selling injectable antibiotic -- continued to grow and new products, such as the AIDS drug Invirase, were very well received by the market.
Birgit Kulhoff of Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) noted a slight slowdown in fourth quarter sales from the pharmaceuticals division, but added this was purely seasonal.
"There is no need to worry, this is only due to seasonal changes," Kulhoff said.
Roche also confirmed that it expected 1996 profits to exceed 1995's net profit of 3.37 billion Swiss francs. Roche will report 1996 results on March 24.
"Taking into account another good result for the group's non-operating activities as well, Roche expects to see consolidated net income increase once again," Roche said in a statement.

Higher drugs sales were achieved not only in North America and Europe -- the two most important markets -- but also in Brazil, Mexico, Australia and other major markets. Solid volume growth in Japan helped offset a decline in revenue from the government's mandated price cuts.
Analysts forecast a 15.7 percent rise in Roche's 1996 group net profit to 3.9 billion from 1995's 3.37 billion.
Boosted by the launch of several new products and increased penetration of recently-launched products, analysts see Roche's 1998 net profit rising 17 percent to 4.58 billion francs.
"There is enough visibility at the operating level to see that Roche can sustain a high level of growth over a number of years," said Michael Sjoestroem of Pictet & Cie.
The Swiss franc's decline against the dollar is also helping profits, noted Susan Haylock of NatWest Securities.
"The currency benefits are already coming through in the fourth quarter and this bodes well for 1997," said Haylock.
Analysts' optimism about Roche's performance in the next few years is largely based on the range of products that are now maturing and ready to attack the market.
Recently introduced products also comfort analysts.

Sjoestroem said first year sales of Invirase, the first of a new generation of AIDS drugs, already exceeded 200 million francs and he expects annual sales to surpass Roche's own forecast for 400 million francs.
Sjoestroem is also looking to Roche's diagnostics division to start contributing with higher profits as products based on the PCR technology finde more widespread use.
Becker's optimism is based on the coming launch of three new drugs, which have the potential to be blockbusters.
Roche will be introducing Posicor, a cardio-vascular drug, Xenical for obesity and Tasmar for Parkinson's disease.
"There is dynamic growth happening at Roche based on a significant change," Becker said, noting people at Roche were very enthusiastic about the potential of the new drugs.
($1=1.3783 Swiss Franc)
